title: Geo Cells
explain: A geo cell is a fixed-address tile of the map. A function turns a latitude and longitude into a cell id (geohash, S2, H3 or a plain grid), so a question about where something is becomes an ordinary key lookup. My one-line framing: any mapping that shrinks a big problem into a small one is sharding, and a cell id is just a shard key for space.
model:
```
(lat, lng) ──cell fn──▶ cell id ──▶ shard / index bucket
nearby(p, r): cells covering the circle ──▶ read each ──▶ filter by exact distance
```

- **Index:** store every object under its cell id.
- **Query:** compute the cells that cover the search circle, read them, then filter by exact distance. Always include the **neighbours**: a point near an edge has neighbours in the next cell. With cell side ≥ radius, the circle touches at most **9 cells** (centre plus 8 neighbours).
- **Cell size is the knob:** small cells give fewer false candidates but more cells per query and more keys; big cells give the reverse.
- **Shard by cell:** the cell id (or a prefix) is the partition key. Dense cities create hot cells, so use **hierarchical** cells (quadtree, S2 levels) and subdivide busy cells adaptively.

Caveats: poles and the date line need a real library, and prefix-based cells are discontinuous, so you cannot rely on a prefix match alone. Use cases: ride matching, nearby search, geo-fencing. See [sharding](#/sd/f/sharding) and [partitioning](#/sd/f/partitioning).

details.q: Why is a geo cell a kind of sharding?
details.a: Because it maps a continuous 2-D problem onto discrete keys, so each query touches a small subset of the data instead of everything. That is exactly what a shard key does.

details.q: With 1 km square cells and a 1 km search radius, how many cells can the query circle overlap?
details.a: Up to 9: the circle's diameter is 2 km, which spans up to three cells in each direction. That is why the standard query is the centre cell plus its 8 neighbours.

details.q: Two cabs are 10 m apart on either side of a major boundary, and their geohashes share no prefix. What does that imply?
details.a: Prefix search alone misses neighbours. You must explicitly compute and query adjacent cells (or use a cell system with a covering function), never just look up the prefix.

details.q: How do you choose the cell size?
details.a: From the typical query radius: roughly cell side near the radius, so a query reads about 9 cells. Smaller cells reduce false candidates but multiply cells per query and keys; larger cells return too many candidates to filter.

details.q: 90% of requests come from three downtown cells. What is the fix?
details.a: Use hierarchical cells and split hot cells into smaller children adaptively, so a dense area gets finer cells and a rural one coarse cells. Fixed-size cells cannot balance load; routing by cell id alone would keep three shards overloaded.

details.q: Do you still need an exact distance check?
details.a: Yes. A cell is a coarse filter that gives candidates; the final answer needs a distance computation on the actual coordinates.

prompts.q: Explain how you would find the nearest drivers using geo cells, step by step.
points: Map the rider's location to a cell id
Compute the cells covering the search radius, including neighbours
Read drivers stored under each cell
Filter by exact distance, sort, return top k

prompts.q: Explain why a geo cell is sharding and how to shard a cell index that has hot cities.
points: Cell id is a shard key for space
Fixed cells make dense areas hot
Hierarchical cells split busy cells adaptively
Cell size trades false candidates vs cells per query

prompts.q: What are the traps of geohash prefix search and how do you avoid them?
points: Poles and date line need a library
Exact distance filter at the end
